title: AI Adoption and Firm Performance: Size-Dependent Effects and the Moderating Role of Regional Innovation Ecosystems
authors: Marco Cucculelli (Università Politecnica Delle Marche); Ali Shah (Università Politecnica Delle Marche)
abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) adoption shapes firm performance by combining a large panel of Italian firms observed from 2015 to 2024 with detailed regional indicators of innovation ecosystems. The analysis shows that AI adoption is positively associated with firm growth, both in value added and total factor productivity (TFP). However, the benefits are not evenly distributed across firms. A clear U-shaped pattern emerges: small and large firms achieve the largest performance gains, whereas medium-sized firms benefit less. The regional context further conditions these effects. Firms located in less-developed regions—with weaker innovation infrastructure, lower knowledge creation, and fewer collaboration networks—experience larger performance improvements from adopting AI, suggesting that advanced technologies can substitute for missing external capabilities. Taken together, the results highlight that both organizational scale and regional environments shape the effectiveness of AI deployment. They also indicate that, under the right conditions, AI can support economic convergence by helping lagging firms and regions catch up.

title: The Value of Cross-Product and Cross-Location Information in Demand Forecasting
authors: Rang (Rae) Gong (The Ohio State University); Walter Zinn (The Ohio State University); Xiang (Sean) Wan (The Ohio State University); Keely Croxton (The Ohio State University)
abstract: (a) Purpose of the study/piece: Accurate demand forecasting is fundamental to achieving reliable and efficient operations in supply chains, yet forecasting performance remains limited in many real-world environments characterized by high uncertainty, demand variability, and sparse historical data. Traditional forecasting approaches primarily rely on a product’s own historical demand, which restricts their ability to capture market dynamics shaped by substitution behavior, complementary consumption, and competitive interactions across stores. This research examines whether incorporating cross-product and cross-location information can improve item-level forecasting accuracy and identifies the conditions under which such information provides the greatest value.  (b) Research method: We use a transformer-based time-series framework to incorporate these relational features into the analysis. Product-level substitution and complementary relationships are quantified based on historical co-movement in demand, and cross-location information is represented using demand signals from nearby stores identified by geographic proximity. These relational inputs are compared against baseline models that rely only on an item’s historical demand to assess whether they improve forecasting performance and under what conditions the improvements are most substantial. The analysis uses real-world transactional data from a healthcare services company, including more than 90 million observations across over 2,500 locations and 7,000 products. (c) Findings or Predicted Findings: Preliminary results show that incorporating cross-product and cross-location information yields meaningful improvements in item-level forecasting accuracy compared to models that rely only on each item’s historical demand. At this stage, we have demonstrated the proof-of-concept and will continue to fine-tune the analysis. The next phase of the analysis will examine the contribution of different relationship types individually and use post-hoc analysis to see which relationships contribute more to accuracy improvement. We will then compare forecasting accuracy improvements across different demand environments and relationship configurations, enabling clearer interpretation of when and why relational information is most beneficial. (d) This work shows how research can integrate managerial thinking into algorithm development by embedding real operational relationships directly into the modeling process. The research contributes theoretically by demonstrating that relational information across products and nearby stores holds predictive value and improves forecasting performance compared to treating items independently. From a managerial perspective, more accurate forecasts can support better inventory positioning, reduced stockouts, fewer emergency reallocations, and more responsive replenishment strategies. Additionally, the research helps improve understanding of the root reasons behind customer decision-making behavior by revealing how purchasing patterns reflect underlying relational demand dynamics.

title: When Rareness and Scarcity Interact: Complementary, Substitution, and Conflicting Effects in Resource-Based Competitive Advantage
authors: Temitope Oladimeji (University of Massachusetts Amherst)
abstract: Resource-based theory has long held that resources must be limited in supply to generate competitive advantage. Two distinct traditions emerged—Barney’s emphasis on rareness (the degree to which a resource is possessed by few competing firms) and Peteraf’s emphasis on scarcity (the degree to which aggregate demand exceeds available supply)—which Peteraf and Barney (2003) reconciled as “very nearly the same.” While this phrasing left conceptual space for differences, subsequent literature has often treated rareness and scarcity as completely interchangeable. We refine this reconciliation by showing that while functionally similar, rareness and scarcity operate through sufficiently distinct mechanisms that their interaction creates dynamics interchangeability cannot predict. When resources exhibit both characteristics, three patterns emerge: complementary (mechanisms amplify advantage beyond additive effects), substitution (context determines dominance), and conflicting (mechanisms work at cross-purposes—differentiation creating unfulfillable demand, scarcity preventing network effects, or resource allocation dilemmas reducing net advantage below either alone). Conflicts indicate mechanistic distinction within functional similarity, as identical concepts cannot conflict. We specify boundary conditions determining patterns and examine how resource origins (exogenous versus endogenous) moderate strategic flexibility. Our framework refines Peteraf and Barney’s reconciliation: functional similarity dominates when one mechanism operates; mechanistic distinctions require specification when both operate simultaneously.

title: Resource Redeployment in Entrepreneurial Firms: A Theoretical Model and Empirical Evidence from the Oil-drilling Industry
authors: Arkadiy Sakhartov (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign); Toby Li (Texas A&M University); Jeffrey Reuer (Purdue University)
abstract: Resource redeployment is a resource allocation strategy, or a real option, which involves withdrawing resources from one use and allocating them to another use. Such redeployment was elaborated conceptually and studied empirically. Meanwhile, three serious issues remained unresolved in research. First, research on resource redeployment was restricted to large established (and mostly multi-business) firms, which were even believed to be unique in having the option to redeploy their resources. However, entrepreneurial firms are under strong pressure to efficiently allocate resources, and resource redeployment is one of important strategies to do so. Second, empirical research on resource redeployment never registered it directly. Instead, either some circumstantial evidence was used to operationalize resource redeployment in the available data or the observed choices could not clearly separate resource redeployment from other resource allocation strategies. Finally, the effect of uncertainty, the key determinant of the redeployment option, was poorly understood. On the one hand formal models predicted that the value of the redeployment option is enhanced by uncertainty. On the other hand, verbal theoretical accounts referred to hysteresis present in real options and predicted that such hysteresis results in the negative effect of uncertainty on the use of the redeployment option. This study uses a large sample of entrepreneurial ventures that operate in oil-drilling industry in Texas and can redeploy their rigs across oil fields. The empirical analysis demonstrates that resource redeployment is very prevalent among such firms. In addition to registering redeployment directly, this study empirically relates it to formal predictions of what determines it, including uncertainty.

title: How Does Generative AI Affect Theories of the Firm?
authors: Boyoon Chang (Dartmouth College); Geoffrey Parker (Dartmouth College); Marshall Van Alstyne (Boston University)
abstract: Following Coase’s seminal work on the nature of the firm, academic scholars have sought to understand and define a firm, the rationale for its existence, and its boundaries. With the rise of Generative AI, which brings about transformational changes in resources, constraints, means to perform, and strategic orientation, this paper reviews established theories of the firm--Transaction Cost Economics, Agency Theory, Incomplete Contracts Theory, Resource-Based View, and Platform & Ecosystem Theory--to predict  possible effects of AI on the boundaries, internal structure, and overall functioning of a firm. Generative AI offers new capabilities in content generation, pattern recognition, and learning and improving. We characterize these functions as automating, augmenting, autonomous tasking, hyper-personalizing, and virtualizing. We then examine their effects on key parameters that define the nature of the firm, while challenging foundational assumptions such as bounded rationality and opportunism. We argue that generative AI partially restores rational economic agency at both the individual and firm levels, while introducing new forms of opportunistic behavior. In parallel, we assess the extent to which it may reconfigure existing externalities, contractual arrangements, transaction costs, and processes of knowledge formation. Taken together, we identify key forces at play and develop propositions on governance structures, the resources that become more salient, the likely organizational form of a firm, and the emergence of new inter-firm dynamics. We conclude by discussing whether a new theory is needed in light of these advancements.

title: Beyond Productivity: Evaluating the Hidden Costs of Generative AI in Software Development
authors: Edward Anderson (University of Texas at Austin); Geoffrey Parker (Dartmouth College)
abstract: AI-assisted programming tools are increasingly adopted to enhance developer productivity by automating routine tasks and accelerating software development. While early evidence highlights short-term productivity gains, our study shows that excessive reliance on AI can unintentionally accelerate the accumulation of technical debt, leading to escalating maintenance costs and eventual revenue erosion. Drawing on interviews with software engineers and insights from the literature, we build a dynamic simulation model to examine the long-term impacts of AI-assisted coding under varying conditions of project horizon, legacy-system interaction, developer skill, and market dynamism. Our results reveal that productivity benefits follow an inverted-U pattern: there exists a “sweet spot” where AI assistance improves overall performance, but beyond this threshold, compounded technical debt undermines system maintainability and profitability. We further show that greenfield environments and fast-evolving markets can tolerate higher levels of AI assistance, whereas brownfield (legacy) settings and teams with less skilled developers are substantially more susceptible to long-term decline. We identify technical-debt retirement as a strategic guardrail that can help sustain AI benefits over time. These findings demonstrate that AI-assisted development is not simply a choice of productivity tool, but a strategic decision that must consider programming environment constraints, system longevity, skill composition, and market factors. Finally, we discuss implications for theory and management.

title: The Habitable Zone of Scientific Creativity: Cognitive Distance, Absorptive Capacity, and Impact
authors: Tan Tran (Beyondegrees Sas); Christian Goglin (ICD Business School)
abstract: Originality is widely viewed as a driver of scientific progress, yet evidence on how novelty translates into impact remains mixed. Prior studies emphasize recombination benefits but often overlook how the scientific system’s capacity to interpret novel ideas changes over time. Using 23.1 million life-science articles published between 1824 and 2025, this study examines how disciplinary originality—measured as Average Interdisciplinary Distance (AID)—shapes scientific impact across historical periods. We find a robust inverted-U relationship: moderate disciplinary distance maximizes citations, while both conventional and highly distant work is less influential. Crucially, this relationship is historically dynamic. During the post-war Big Science era, the range of impactful originality broadened, whereas in the digital era it narrowed and became more selective despite high peak impact. These findings show that originality is rewarded only within historically contingent “habitable zones” defined by the scientific system’s collective absorptive capacity. The study contributes to innovation research by linking recombination, absorptive capacity, and long-run structural change in science.

title: Rebirth from Disrepute:  Overcoming Legitimacy Bottleneck for Innovation Ecosystem Creation in the Context of Industry Re-emergence
authors: Runjin Guo (Zhejiang University); Yining Luo (Zhejiang University)
abstract:
As the concept of ecosystem receives increasing attention in managerial research, overcoming key bottlenecks during ecosystem creation remains a persistent challenge. Existing empirical research has primarily examined large-scale or mature ecosystems with stable elements (Adner, 2017), often overlooking how ecosystems emerge from re-emerging industry contexts, where the unique conditions and barriers to ecosystem creation remain underexplored. When creating an ecosystem in a re-emerging industry, cognitive legacies from the past and the challenge of articulating a compelling vision for the future often constitute a significant hurdle—what we refer to as a “legitimacy bottleneck”. Thus we ask: How can the legitimacy bottleneck be overcome when creating an innovation ecosystem in the context of industry re-emergence?

Through a case study of the Dendrobium officinale industry, a kind of traditional Chinese Medicine, we uncover the mechanism of how ecosystem actors emerge and interact to overcome the legitimacy bottleneck and facilitate the ecosystem creation. Following Yin (2009) and Gioia et al. (2013) method, we collect data from semi-structured interviews and archives, develop chronologies of events, recognize structures of ecosystem actors at each temporal phase, and develop aggregated themes to identify key mechanisms. We develop a process model that highlights the three phases of innovation ecosystem creation and legitimacy bottleneck resolution in industry re-emergence context, including modernization, destigmatization and legitimization. Technological upgrading in the modernization phase enabled ecosystem emergence; when legitimacy bottleneck emerges due to fraud scandal, the government was involved in to push industry standardization, stigma reduction and social cognition enhancement; finally, broader actor participation in the legitimization phase supported category reframing and market expansion.

Our findings illustrate how an innovation ecosystem gradually forms within a legacy industry, outlining the processes and temporal sequencing of its developmental phases, thereby enriching the literature on ecosystem evolution in nascent contexts. On the one hand, we offer empirical evidence of how an innovation ecosystem is created gradually within a legacy industry. Our study sharpens the understanding of how extant actors in an ecosystem introduce or cultivate new organizations to build the ecosystem capability portfolio. On the other hand, our finding extends industrial legitimacy literature by identifying the legitimacy bottleneck and revealing how key actors emerge and interact dynamically to overcome it, thus brings attention to the source and resolution of legitimacy bottleneck ecosystem may face in re-emerging industries.

References
Adner, R. 2017. Ecosystem as Structure: An Actionable Construct for Strategy. Journal of Management, 43(1), 39–58.
Gioia, D. A., Corley, K. G., & Hamilton, A. L. 2013. Seeking Qualitative Rigor in Inductive Research: Notes on the Gioia Methodology. Organizational Research Methods, 16(1), 15–31. 
Yin, R. K. 2009. Case Study Research: Design and Methods. SAGE Publications.

title: Timing University Entry: Institutional Pressures and Semiconductor Research Adoption
authors: Shuqi Sun (Arizona State University); Maryann Feldman (Arizona State University)
abstract:
Universities have become central players in regional innovation ecosystems, extending beyond traditional education and research roles to actively engage with emerging technology fields. As universities navigate this expanded mission, they face critical strategic decisions about when and how to enter new research domains, shaped by institutional pressures and peer behavior. This study addresses two research questions: First, when and where did U.S. universities enter semiconductor research, and how did entry patterns evolve? Second, do universities enter in response to peer institutions' entry, and are peer effects stronger for geographically proximate and higher-status peers?
First, we explore the temporal evolution of university entry into semiconductor research, examining temporal distribution distinguishing early versus late entrants, geographic distribution of engaged universities, and clustering patterns. We construct a novel dataset linking Scopus publication data and USPTO patent data. By matching inventor names on patents to university author names, we comprehensively track university engagement in semiconductor research. Second, we investigate university entry strategies through mimetic pressures based on institutional theory, capturing these pressures through peer universities' publication activity and comparing effects from national versus in-state peers, and examining how peer status shapes influence.
This research makes three contributions: First, we examine semiconductor research from the university perspective rather than the traditional firm-centric view. Second, we apply institutional theory to explain university strategic behavior in emerging technology fields, providing a new lens for understanding university research strategies. Third, we demonstrate a methodological approach integrating patent and publication data for comprehensive tracking of university engagement.

title: Are Shrinking Clusters Bad for Everyone? The Positive Externalities of Shrinking Clusters for Entrepreneurial Firms
authors: Min Guo (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign); Min Jung  Kim (Korea University)
abstract: Research in strategy and entrepreneurship has long focused on large, growing industry clusters, examining how high geographic concentration of industry activity generates positive externalities for firm performance. However, this growth-only perspective overlooks the temporal dynamics of clusters, specifically periods of decline where industry concentration decreases. While a decline is often viewed negatively, this study asks: Are shrinking clusters bad for everyone? We investigate the positive externalities of shrinking clusters, specifically examining how entrepreneurs, particularly minority entrepreneurs who suffer from severe resource constraints, can benefit from cluster decline. We propose that the decline of an industry cluster, as incumbent firms exit or relocate, releases cluster-specific resources, such as human capital, venture funding, and organizational relationships, that are not easily transferable across geographic boundaries. While these resources are geographically sticky, they are often transferable to related industries in the same region. Consequently, these freed-up resources become available to local entrepreneurs in related industries. Thus, we propose that the decline of an industry cluster increases both new venture creation and venture growth in related industries in the same region. Moreover, because minority entrepreneurs face greater barriers to accessing high-quality resources, we propose that this positive relationship is stronger for ventures founded by minority entrepreneurs. This research contributes to the literature by moving beyond a growth-only perspective to a holistic view of cluster dynamics and helps policymakers design policies to leverage industry decline for local economic growth.

title: From Tolerance to Termination: How Venture Capitalists Decide on Startups’ Invention Failures
authors: Shu Deng (University of Mississippi); Jung H. Kwon (University of Denver)
abstract:
Venture capitalists (VCs) routinely face the challenge of deciding whether to persist in or terminate investments as new information about startup performance unfolds. In innovation-driven contexts, this decision is particularly complex because technological experimentation inevitably generates invention failures that are ambiguous in their implications—startups’ invention failure can either serve as a signal of learning or a trigger of abandonment. Little is known about when and why failure sustains versus undermines investor commitment. We address this puzzle by conceptualizing VC follow-on investment decisions as an optimal stopping problem in which investors balance the informational value of waiting against the costs of continued commitment.
We develop a formal model in which VCs observe new information about startups’ invention activities and follow threshold-based rules governing investment continuation and termination. The model predicts a non-monotonic relationship between invention failure and investment termination: moderate failure enhances learning and increases the value of waiting, whereas very low or excessive failure reduces expected future payoffs and accelerates exit. Importantly, the model also predicts systematic heterogeneity in stopping thresholds across investors, shaped by differences in experiential depth and breadth.
We test these predictions using a novel dataset that links U.S. venture capital investments to detailed patent application outcomes. Analyzing 16,013 funding rounds involving 2,328 VCs and 3,392 startups from 2002 to 2022, we find robust evidence of a U-shaped relationship between startups’ invention failure rates and the likelihood of VC investment termination. Consistent with optimal stopping logic, termination likelihood is lowest at intermediate levels of failure. Moreover, this relationship varies systematically with investor experience. VCs with deeper technological or industrial familiarity exhibit greater tolerance for invention failure, shifting termination thresholds rightward, whereas VCs with broader experience across technologies or industries terminate investments at lower levels of failure due to higher opportunity costs.
These findings contribute to research on entrepreneurial experimentation, venture capital decision-making, and strategic persistence by offering a dynamic, forward-looking explanation for failure tolerance. By framing investment continuation and exit as optimal timing decisions, this study reconciles competing views of failure and highlights how investor experience conditions the strategic meaning of negative innovation signals. Practically, the results underscore that effective governance of entrepreneurial experimentation depends not only on observing failure, but on interpreting its magnitude and timing relative to investors’ capabilities and opportunity sets.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Teaching STEM Graduate Students Entrepreneurship, Family Business Governance, and Scaling to Global Family Conglomerates
authors: John Lecounte (St John Fisher University )
abstract: During this study, I conducted a systematic literature review to develop a comprehensive theoretical framework for teaching entrepreneurship to Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) students. Drawing upon the theoretical foundations of Experiential Learning Theory (Kolb, 1984), Constructivist Theory (Piaget, 1971; Vygotsky, 1978), Cognitivism Theory (Bruner, 1966; 1971), Social Identity Theory (Tajfel et al., 1979), Achievement Motivation Theory (McClelland, 1961; 1976), Theory of Economic Development (Schumpeter, 1934; 1942), Human Capital Theory (Becker, 1976; 1993), and Expectancy Theory (Vroom, 1964), the study synthesizes interdisciplinary perspectives from education, psychology, economics, and entrepreneurship. The integration of entrepreneurship and STEM education has become a critical and rapidly evolving area of scholarship, necessitating a comprehensive review from multiple perspectives (Yu et al., 2025). At the micro level, entrepreneurial career development describes the process by which individuals perceive entrepreneurship as a meaningful professional pathway (Ozyazici et al., 2025), emphasizing the transferability of STEM competencies such as problem decomposition, analytical reasoning, and innovation to entrepreneurial contexts. The proposed framework prioritizes experiential, cognitively scaffolded, and socially embedded learning approaches that foster the development of an entrepreneurial mindset, strategic thinking, governance competence, and emotional maturity. In alignment with the academy’s mission to advance knowledge and demonstrate societal value, this study contributes to the fields of entrepreneurship and family business management by presenting a theoretically grounded framework for teaching STEM graduate students’ entrepreneurship, family business governance, and the scaling of Global Family Conglomerates.

title: The Institutional Economics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Higher Education: A Transaction Cost Analysis of University Transformation
authors: Pelin Bicen (Suffolk University )
abstract:
Why do universities persist in their current bundled form - integrating research, teaching, credentialing, and socialization within hierarchical organizations - when alternative arrangements for knowledge production and transmission have proliferated? This paper applies transaction cost economics (TCE) to answer this question and to analyze how artificial intelligence (AI) may fundamentally transform the institutional logic of higher education. While canonical organization theories describe how universities function internally - as loosely coupled systems (Weick, 1976), legitimacy-seeking entities (Meyer & Rowan, 1977), or organized anarchies (Cohen, March, & Olsen, 1972) - they do not explain why the bundled form emerged and persists. TCE provides this foundation (Coase, 1937; Williamson, 1985), demonstrating that universities internalize functions whose coordination through markets would be prohibitively costly due to verification challenges, monitoring difficulties, appropriability problems (Teece, 1986), and the tacit nature of professional knowledge transfer (Polanyi, 1966).

The paper makes three contributions to organization theory. First, it extends TCE into higher education, developing a systematic account of why credentialing solves signaling problems in labor markets characterized by information asymmetry (Spence, 1973; Akerlof, 1970), why instruction addresses monitoring challenges that market-based provision cannot resolve (Nelson, 1970), why research bundling enables knowledge appropriation under weak intellectual property conditions (Arrow, 1962; Teece, 1986), and why socialization transfers tacit expertise that resists market coordination (Lave & Wenger, 1991). Second, and more fundamentally, the paper advances transaction cost theory by distinguishing between marginal and parametric technological effects on governance structures. Prior technologies - printing, broadcasting, the internet - produced marginal effects: they reduced certain transaction costs while leaving the fundamental parameters that favor bundled governance intact. This explains why universities absorbed these technologies without institutional displacement, and why MOOCs failed to disrupt traditional institutions despite initial predictions (Hoxby, 2014; Reich & Ruipérez-Valiente, 2019). Artificial intelligence differs because it transforms the parameters themselves. AI does not merely make monitoring cheaper; it changes what monitoring means when human and machine contributions become indistinguishable (Cotton, Cotton, & Shipway, 2023). AI does not simply reduce information asymmetry; it creates new forms of asymmetry regarding algorithmic processes while dissolving traditional asymmetries regarding expert knowledge (Agrawal, Gans, & Goldfarb, 2018).

Third, the paper integrates TCE with institutional theory (DiMaggio & Powell, 1983) to explain organizational persistence and change under technological disruption. The analysis yields a typology that maps university functions according to AI substitutability and verification complexity, generating propositions about which institutional arrangements face displacement (content delivery, routine assessment), which gain distinctive importance (professional identity formation, ethical development, research apprenticeship), and which become contested terrain where institutions and markets compete on verification capacity (complex skill development, collaborative capabilities). The framework provides principled criteria for distinguishing between functions that remain essential - continuing to solve transaction cost problems AI does not address - and those that are historically contingent, persisting only through legitimacy and inertia.

For industry studies scholars, this paper demonstrates how transaction cost analysis can illuminate institutional transformation in knowledge-intensive industries facing technological disruption. The distinction between marginal and parametric technological effects has implications far beyond higher education, providing theoretical grounding for understanding why some technologies produce incremental adaptation while others precipitate genuine institutional transformation (Langlois, 2003). For policymakers navigating AI's impact on the higher education industry, the framework offers tools for anticipating which institutional arrangements will prove durable and which require fundamental reconceptualization - a question of considerable consequence as institutions, employers, and governments grapple with AI's implications for workforce development, credentialing, and knowledge production.

title: Political Entrepreneurs: Are Entrepreneurs in Politics Entrepreneurial in Policymaking?
authors: Joyce Ma (The Fuqua School of Business, Duke University); Aaron Chatterji (The Fuqua School of Business, Duke University); Jorge  Guzman (Columbia Business School, Columbia University); Ryan Mcdevitt (The Fuqua School of Business, Duke University)
abstract: Business interests influence public policy through lobbying and campaign contributions, yet business owners can also shape policy by entering elected office themselves. How does entrepreneurial experience shape policymaking once entrepreneurs become legislators? This paper examines whether entrepreneurs in legislative office behave differently from other legislators and whether they advance broad business interests or a distinct entrepreneurial policy agenda. We construct a novel dataset linking personal financial disclosures of state legislators to comprehensive legislative records from 26 U.S. states between 2009 and 2023. Using detailed information on business ownership and employment, we identify legislators with entrepreneurial backgrounds and link them to the bills they sponsor. Applying large language models to bill texts, we classify legislation as pro-business or pro-entry and measure the volume, share, and intensity of such bills. We further benchmark legislative agendas using bills supported by state Chambers of Commerce. We find that entrepreneurial representation varies primarily across states and is negatively associated with legislative professionalism and state-level entrepreneurial activity, consistent with the idea that opportunity costs discourage entrepreneurs from holding office. Once elected, entrepreneurs are not more prolific sponsors overall but are significantly more likely to initiate legislation as first primary sponsors. They also do not act as broad representatives of business interests; instead, they selectively advance pro-entry policies, focusing on antitrust and deregulation. These findings highlight an insider channel of political engagement of business interests and show how entrepreneurial experience shapes legislative agenda by targeting barriers to market entry rather than advancing generic pro-business issues.

title: Measuring Regional Markets for Innovation Space
authors: Utkarsha Dahal (University of Southern Mississippi); Christopher Smith (University of Southern Mississippi)
abstract:
The measurement of innovation activity and its economic impact traditionally has focused on employment and industrial output indicators. However, these metrics have some notable limitations. One limitation is they do not account for the capacity-building processes within innovation ecosystems which comprise a significant aspect of innovation activity. For example, capital expenditures on facilities to support research, development, and commercialization activities are not reflected in such indicators. Investment in innovation facilities are real estate market events which can affect prices of adjacent real estate properties. They also send important signals about the expansion of innovation capacity to ecosystem stakeholders. Such signals can spur demand for adjacent real estate properties which may be captured in price trends. Investment in innovation facilities may also entice new real estate development projects. Innovation facilities may also induce new foot traffic patterns both for the facility and for neighboring establishments. Current approaches to measuring innovation activity leave innovation researchers without the ability to incorporate the information provided by such capacity-building activity into their analysis and planning. 

This paper fill this information gap by analyzing regional markets for R&D (research and development) space. Although it is a niche market, the demand and supply of R&D space send important signals about future innovation ecosystem performance. The future demand for R&D space provides useful information about the attractiveness of a community to firms involved in technology-based innovation activities. Similarly, the projected supply of R&D space provides information about local growth of innovation capacity and about the likelihood of a future surplus or deficit of supply. This information can help guide the plans of developers and policymakers.

title: How Entrepreneurial Ecosystems Shape Startup Exit under Macro-Institutional Shocks
authors: Indu Khurana (Hampden-Sydney College); Ananya Sheth (Cal Poly)
abstract: We examine how entrepreneurial ecosystems shape startup exit under macro-institutional shocks. Prior research treats exit as a firm-level outcome, paying less attention to how ecosystem structure conditions which exit pathways remain viable as institutional conditions shift. We argue that ecosystems shape exit through two structural properties. First, exit pathways differ in institutional exposure—the degree to which successful exit depends on politically contingent, formally regulated, and cross-border institutional arrangements. Among the two main harvest exit pathways, Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) exhibit high exposure, whereas acquisitions are comparatively buffered. Second, entrepreneurial ecosystems vary in exit pathway concentration—some concentrate exit activity around a single dominant pathway; others support multiple viable routes. Using 1,572 battery technology startups founded in the United States and China between 1990 and 2024, we examine the impact of rising U.S.-China tension as a macro-institutional shock on exit outcomes. In ecosystems with diversified exit pathways, bilateral tension more than doubles IPO likelihood and accelerates time to IPO by approximately ten years. In ecosystems with concentrated exit pathways, bilateral tension reduces IPO likelihood by 29 percent, and this acceleration does not occur, resulting in a 14-year divergence in IPO timing across ecosystem types. Acquisition exits remain unaffected regardless of exit pathway concentration, consistent with their lower institutional exposure. These findings articulate a macro–meso–micro linkage by showing how ecosystem exit pathway concentration moderates the impact of macro-institutional shocks on firm-level exit through institutionally exposed pathways.

title: Synthetic Creativity and Human Talents: How Generative AI Reshapes Value in the Music Industry
authors: Mingtao Xu (Tsinghua University); Fan Yang (Tsinghua University)
abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into creative industries challenges conventional valuations of human capital. This study investigates how the revelation of AI-generated content reshapes perceived value in the music industry. Leveraging the natural experiment of a trending musician’s AI nature revelation, we employ a difference-in-differences strategy to estimate how audience engagement changes once they learn the act is AI-generated. Our results reveal a significant algorithm aversion among audiences, with negative sentiment spilling over to adjacent human musicians. Musicians in genres perceived as low in humanity experience a relative decline in engagement compared to those in high-humanity genres, with those stylistically closer to AI suffering greater losses. Furthermore, musicians with less established career capital are disproportionately affected. Our findings demonstrate AI's context-dependent impact and provide a framework for understanding evolving work and valuation structures in the arts.

title: The Power and Pitfalls of Techno-Industrial Policy: Evidence from China
authors: Hannah Wei (IMF)
abstract: I study how industrial policy shapes innovation by examining China's Strategic and Emerging Industries (SEI) initiative (2010-2018), a large-scale fiscal intervention targeting frontier technology sectors. Employing a staggered difference-in-differences design with city-industry-level patent data, I uncover three key findings: (1) While patent quantity surged by 184%, quality metrics showed minimal improvement; (2) The quantity gains came at a 14% decrease in patent output from untreated sectors, revealing sectoral displacement instead of crowd-in effects; (3) Cities that adopted path-dependent targeting (selecting sectors with pre-existing innovation advantages) achieved over twice the patent growth rates of their counterparts, though without corresponding quality gains. These findings reveal a paradox in China's development model: while achieving unprecedented success in scaling innovation quantity, the nation has yet to realize comparable quality gains - a critical gap as it transitions from 'made' to 'created in China'.

title: Latent Hazards: Counterperformative Effects of Certification in New Ventures
authors: Scott Taylor (University of Southern California)
abstract: New firms invest heavily in legitimacy to mobilize stakeholder resources. Consistent with institutional theory, certification is widely argued, and empirically shown, to confer legitimacy and unlock resources from wary audiences. Yet we know far less about when certification can backfire, especially for young ventures. I investigate how certifications can constrain the very resources they were meant to enhance, a process I call certification counterperformativity. Using a qualitative embedded case study of ethical certifications in the cosmetics industry, I illustrate how certifications can embed latent hazards that remain largely invisible at adoption but later become consequential when firms attempt to innovate, scale, expand geographically, or respond to shifting market expectations. Through a thematic analysis of interviews, fieldwork, archival documents, and public statements from informants positioned along the product value chain, I develop a process model explaining how latent hazards (internal friction, operational strain, and strategic rigidity) are activated by subsequent firm initiatives and/or external shifts in standards, stakeholder preferences, and certification governance. Once activated, these hazards generate counterperformative outcomes that can erode flexibility, slow execution, and narrow strategic options, thereby undermining the very legitimacy and resource access certification initially helped secure. In doing so, I primarily contribute to certification research by theorizing certification not only as a legitimacy mechanism, but also as a potential source of deferred constraint, clarifying how and when an apparently beneficial signal can turn into a binding liability for new ventures. Second, as a tertiary contribution, this study contributes to entrepreneurship research by reframing early legitimacy-seeking as an intertemporal strategic tradeoff, showing how decisions made to secure external validation can introduce path dependencies that shape and potentially constrain new ventures’ future strategic trajectories.

title: Multimodal Optimal Distinctiveness
authors: Rui Wang (Tsinghua University); Joel Gehman (George Washington University)
abstract:
How do entrepreneurs convey the distinctiveness of their ventures without compromising categorical comprehension? Drawing on optimal distinctiveness and multimodality studies, we introduce the concept of “multimodal optimal distinctiveness” and theorize how visual and verbal modes serve complementary functions that jointly help entrepreneurs achieve optimal distinctiveness. Analyzing data from over 140,000 Kickstarter campaigns and employing state-of-the-art foundation models, we find that visual distinctiveness (conformity) negatively (positively) relates to funding outcomes, while verbal distinctiveness positively relates to funding outcomes. Moreover, the positive effect of verbal distinctiveness is strongest when visual distinctiveness is low, suggesting that modalities serve complementary functions—visuals anchor category comprehension while text articulates differentiation. 

We further examine how category heterogeneity—the variance of distinctiveness within a category—moderates these relationships. In homogeneous categories where prototypes are well-defined, verbal distinctiveness shows a monotonically positive effect; the category itself serves as an evaluation anchor. In heterogeneous categories where audience expectations are diffuse, verbal distinctiveness exhibits a U-shaped pattern: moderate distinctiveness underperforms relative to either strong conformity or bold differentiation. These findings suggest that the conformity-distinctiveness trade-off is contingent on the strength of categorical anchors available to audiences.              

Our findings advance a multimodal view of optimal distinctiveness in which different modalities are not interchangeable but complementary in satisfying the dual needs for fitting in and standing out. Our study suggests that the conformity-distinctiveness trade-off need not be a balancing act but rather a design problem that can be resolved through strategic deployment of cultural means across modalities.

title: Stars vs. Centrality: What Matters in New Digital Product Development Teams?
authors: Karthik Ramachandran (Georgia Institute of Technology)
abstract:
We examine how team composition mechanisms, specifically the presence of stars (i.e., high performers) and centrally connected members, shape performance outcomes in new digital product development. Using the video game industry as an innovative setting, we test whether stars are essential for success or whether team members with central connections can provide comparable benefits and substitute for stars.

We assemble a dataset of video game development projects and map collaboration ties from industry credits to construct measures of stardom and network position (including PageRank centrality). We link these team characteristics to new product sales and estimate their effects using causal inference techniques, confirming results across specifications.

Our findings reveal that while stars enhance performance, their presence is not essential in this industry. Instead, centrally connected individuals diminish the impact of stars, illustrating a substitutive relationship between stardom and centrality. Well-connected members act as a human platform that aggregates ties, facilitates information sharing, and connects teams to the larger developer ecosystem, helping firms manage risk and uncertainty in hit-driven markets.

These results contribute to research on innovation and new digital product development by clarifying when network position matters more than star power in assembling product teams. They also offer practical guidance for resourcing and staffing decisions: firms should consider the substitutive relationship between centrality and stardom when making recruitment strategies, team design decisions, and resource allocation for product development. Hiring someone with strong connections can deliver similar results, often at lower cost.

title: Seeding Translational Research: Evidence from Corporate Scientist Migration to Academia
authors: Jungkyu Suh (New York University)
abstract: Why are scientific discoveries with academic origins harder to commercialize than those from corporate labs? We hypothesize that universities prioritize the pursuit of codified scientific knowledge at the expense of practical techniques required to exploit natural phenomena in a scalable fashion. In Joel Mokyr's terms, "prescriptive" knowledge in academia is a secondary concern to the mission of accumulating "propositional" knowledge. We test our theory by showing how a group of corporate scientists migrating into U.S. universities facilitated the commercialization of extant academic research. Using the career histories of 691 former corporate scientists moving to universities on LinkedIn from 2000-2022, we identify 1,280 faculty that coauthor with such "corporate migrants" after their arrival. To isolate the effect of "prescriptive" corporate knowledge, we focus on academics' papers written prior to the migrant's arrival and use Coarsened Exact Matching to identify "control" papers close by with similar commercial potential and within the same field. Difference-in-differences estimates suggest that papers "shocked" by corporate migrants receive 115% more citations by patents compared to control papers (relative to the sample mean). Unobserved scientific quality differences do not seem to drive this result as no comparable effect is found for placebo papers exposed to migrants from other universities. We also find that the added patent citations are not more likely to come from migrants’ former employers, ruling out the possibility that the effect merely reflects redirected corporate attention. Rather, the effect is driven by academic papers shocked by migrants with prior knowledge in high-value scientific instruments, suggesting that the transfer of corporate "prescriptive" knowledge aids with commercializing hitherto impractical academic knowledge. Together, our results suggest that academic research is a poor substitute for "prescriptive" knowledge nurtured at corporate laboratories.

title: A Lab-Grown Diamond is Forever… Too: Sustainability-Focused Competition and Ecosystem Reconfiguration in the Global Diamond Jewelry Industry
authors: Melissa Appleyard (Portland State University); Kristi Yuthas (Portland State University)
abstract:
The diamond jewelry industry is undergoing a profound structural transformation as laboratory-grown diamonds (LGDs) have transitioned from niche substitutes to mainstream luxury centerpieces. By 2026, LGDs have captured over half of the U.S. engagement ring market, occurring alongside extreme wholesale price volatility. This disruption, originally rooted in the ethical legacy of "blood diamonds," has evolved into a complex institutional struggle over the definition of sustainability and value.

We introduce the Sustainability-Focused Substitute Ecosystem (SSE) framework to analyze this transition across three pillars. First, we examine supply-focused changes, where the decoupling of production from geological scarcity—facilitated by technological democratization—has led to significant price compression and margin shifts. Second, we analyze institution-focused changes, where new standards such as SCS-007 have enabled both lab-grown and mined diamonds to compete on metrics of carbon neutrality and verified origin. Third, we explore demand-focused changes, where consumer value propositions are being reshaped by the interaction of ethical provenance, product transparency, and shifting perceptions of rarity.

Applying the SSE framework to this longitudinal case, we demonstrate how sustainability has become a contested strategic frame used by both incumbents and disruptors to navigate price volatility and institutional pressure. This analysis provides a tool for understanding how established industries negotiate a new equilibrium when a technologically-driven substitute challenges the fundamental logic of their value chain and market legitimacy.

title: Bridging the Deployment Gap: Regional Variance in AI Operationalization and the Drift Compatibility Model
authors: Meena Al-Azzawe (Kinaxis); Melissa Appleyard (Portland State University); Kristi Yuthas (Portland State University)
abstract:
Industry and policy analyses report a widening gap in AI operationalization: while North America dominates frontier model development, organizations in the Asia-Pacific region are integrating these systems more rapidly into core workflows. These differences persist despite North America’s structural digital maturity and cannot be fully explained by infrastructure or access to talent alone.

We propose that an important sociotechnical variable is the institutional orientation toward determinism and variance. Classical automation and machine-learning pipelines prioritize process control. Deviations require corrective action to maintain stability. Modern AI systems challenge this paradigm at its foundation; instead of eliminating variance, they express it. Generative models produce outputs by sampling from probability distributions. Agentic AI orchestrates reasoning chains that dynamically adjust intermediate actions based on environmental cues, internal heuristics, or updated goals. We term this inherent output variability "drift"—the natural fluctuation in AI system behavior that stems from probabilistic architectures rather than system failure or degradation. AI deployment introduces new forms of organizational burden that cannot be resolved through technical optimization alone. The movement from deterministic architectures to probabilistic systems requires corresponding changes in organizational cognition, variance-processing norms, and governance structures.

In this paper, we explore how variance-processing capabilities shape AI adoption and introduce the Drift Compatibility Model, a framework that integrates these insights for predicting alignment with probabilistic AI systems. Using this framework, we conceptualize how organizations can interpret, absorb, and leverage drift. This work can inform AI governance and deployment strategies.

title: Coopetition in Charging Infrastructure
authors: Sanchari Guha Niyogi (Institute of Management and Technology, Hyderabad); Prasenjit Mandal (Neoma Business School); Abhishek Roy (Temple University); Abhishek Chakraborty (Xlri Jamshedpur)
abstract: The rapid growth of the Electric Vehicle (EV) market is fundamentally constrained by a fragmented charging infrastructure, characterized by the coexistence of multiple proprietary standards (e.g., NACS, CCS). This fragmentation creates consumer range anxiety, complicates strategic investments for automakers, and hinders mass EV adoption. Our research investigates the strategic decision of open-access standardization, where an innovator (e.g., Tesla) allows an imitator (e.g., Ford) to utilize its proprietary charging network: a form of coopetition driven by the innovator’s potential for data monetization. We develop an analytical model that integrates the operational decisions of physical infrastructure investment with the strategic opportunity of monetizing vehicle usage data. Our analysis characterizes the equilibrium investment and access strategies for both firms. We establish that open access is a contingent equilibrium strategy that can generate win-win outcomes for both firms only when the innovator’s data monetization potential is sufficiently high and the imitator’s independent infrastructure is relatively inefficient. Counter-intuitively, we find that the prospect of open access can reduce the innovator’s incentive to expand its physical network, as the core strategic value shifts from physical scale to the depth of collected data. Finally, our social welfare analysis reveals that consumer surplus and total welfare are maximized only under conditions of mutual investment and open access (coopetition), as this configuration simultaneously improves network coverage, alleviates congestion, and ensures interoperability. This study provides critical operational and strategic insights for automakers on optimal network design and standardization, and for policymakers seeking to maximize EV adoption through infrastructure mandates.

title: Mapping the Evolution of Entrepreneurship as a Scientific Discipline: A Sixty-Year Bibliometric and Network Analysis (1960–2020)
authors: Claudia Gonzalez Brambila (ITAM)
abstract:
This study examines the evolution and consolidation of entrepreneurship as a scientific discipline through a comprehensive bibliometric and network analysis of publications indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database between 1960 and 2020. The dataset comprises 76,448 cleaned and validated records after filtering an initial sample of 144,861 documents that included articles, proceedings, and meeting papers. The analysis quantifies scientific productivity, disciplinary intersections, and co-authorship dynamics across six decades.
The findings show that entrepreneurship has progressively evolved from a marginal topic in economics and business toward a multidisciplinary domain connected to over 120 research areas, including engineering, education, environmental sciences, and emerging fields such as medical ethics and sports sciences. The United States, China, and the United Kingdom are identified as the most prolific contributors. Network visualizations reveal a growing density of collaborations, particularly after 2000, when the co-authorship network exhibits clear consolidation and the emergence of large, interconnected research communities.
Three econometric models were estimated to assess the influence of network characteristics on individual researchers’ productivity and impact. The results indicate that both the number of distinct co-authors (degree) and the frequency of repeated collaborations have significant positive effects on publication output and citations, while centrality measures (betweenness and eigenvector) show differentiated relationships with productivity and impact. The study confirms the cumulative and collaborative nature of scientific knowledge in entrepreneurship and highlights the critical role of sustained co-authorship in shaping the field’s global research structure.

title: From Fragmentation to Scale: A Corporate Center Blueprint for Enterprise AI
authors: Sami Ghaddar (University of Connecticut); Paul Magill (University of Connecticut)
abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is pushing diversified firms to rethink the corporate center because capabilities can be reused across business units, while failures can create portfolio-wide exposure. Managers face a hybrid design problem: what the corporate center should own versus what should remain with business units, and how standards and escalation can safeguard the enterprise without becoming a bottleneck.

This paper proposes a corporate-center operating blueprint for enterprise AI. The blueprint decomposes AI transformation into discrete activities (data governance, platform/toolchain choices, model deployment, monitoring and incident response, vendor integration) and maps decision authority and execution ownership between the corporate center and business units. It specifies risk-tiered minimum requirements and conditional escalation triggers intended to keep low-risk use cases fast while reserving deeper scrutiny for high-stakes deployments.

The paper is grounded in a structured review of AI-related disclosures in SEC filings for S&P 100 companies (2023-2025). We extract and code AI-related passages from Forms 10-K (Item 1A Risk Factors; Item 7 MD&A) and proxy statements (DEF 14A), capturing: 1) AI framed as enterprise capability, 2) AI framed as enterprise risk, and 3) governance and decision-rights language (board and committee oversight, management accountability, enterprise standards versus local discretion, escalation cues). Publicly documented AI incidents are used to motivate governance mechanisms and boundary conditions. The intended contribution is a practitioner-usable decision-rights map linking corporate strategy research on headquarters design to enterprise AI scaling across industries.

title: Lean Thinking, Deep Impact?  Early Exploration Strategies and Commercialization of Deeptech Ventures
authors: Vinay Subramanian (Wharton)
abstract:
This paper examines how early exploration strategies, sequential or parallel, shape the financial and innovation trajectories of deeptech ventures. These firms must navigate multiple dimensions of uncertainty, including technological feasibility. Moreover, they rely on physical assets to commercialize, making exploration costly. Prior research on entrepreneurial strategy emphasizes experimentation to resolve uncertainty but largely focuses on asset-light settings such as software. Even lean startup methods, which encourage early commercial exploration, are better suited to digital ventures where uncertainty is primarily market-based. Consequently, less is known about the implications of exploration strategy in high-uncertainty, asset-intensive environments. I assembled a novel longitudinal dataset of 13,790 hardware-oriented ventures using primary and archival sources, augmented by machine learning and NLP. Employing multiple empirical strategies, including an exogenous technological development (3D printing), the study finds that parallel exploration improves early commercial outcomes by accelerating market learning and mitigating information frictions, yet risks premature technological lock-in. In contrast, sequential exploration fosters deeper learning, yielding long-run financial and innovation performance.
These results highlight the trade-offs faced by boundedly rational entrepreneurs as they balance resolving uncertainty with enhancing organizational learning. The study extends research on entrepreneurial strategy and experimentation to asset-intensive contexts and delineates the boundary conditions under which lean methods are effective in scaling science and technology ventures.

title: Service Design and Innovation for Aging Societies: Introducing Silver Prosperity Index (SPI)
authors: Rohit Verma (University of South Carolina), Kejia Hu (University of Oxford), Xin Ding (Rutgers University), and Diep Pham (University of South Carolina)
abstract: This paper presents the Silver Prosperity Index (SPI), a data-driven framework for evaluating service innovation in aging societies. The SPI is structured around four pillars: Economic Empowerment, Health and Well-being, Social Cohesion and Connectivity, and Security and Protection. It integrates primary survey data with secondary datasets, applying standardized normalization, confirmatory factor weighting, and cross-validation to ensure reliability. A 2025 application across all 50 U.S. states demonstrates its ability to generate detailed, localized insights. Results demonstrate significant regional disparities in support for aging populations, particularly in digital access, workforce participation, and community resilience. These gaps signal opportunities for developing innovative services targeting older adults.
